lead.t: A short generalised seizure with fever in a child aged 6 months to 5 years, with a quick recovery and an obvious source, is a simple febrile seizure.

snip.t: A short generalised seizure with fever in a child aged 6 months to 5 years, with a quick recovery and an obvious source, is a simple febrile seizure.

Seizure disorder is a general term that is usually used to include any one of several disorders, including epilepsy, febrile seizures, and, possibly, single seizures and symptomatic seizures secondary to metabolic, infectious, or other etiologies.

Febrile seizures are seizures that occur between the ages of 6 and 60 mo (peak 12-18 mo) with a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher, that are not the result of CNS infection or any metabolic imbalance, and that occur in the absence of a history of prior afebrile seizures.
A simple febrile seizure is a primary generalized, usually tonic-clonic, attack associated with fever, lasting for a maximum of 15 min, and not recurrent within a 24-hr period.
Topics: neonatal jaundice, growth, immunisation, diarrhoea and dehydration, pneumonia, malnutrition, febrile seizures, congenital heart disease, nephrotic syndrome, anaemia and childhood infections.
| Febrile seizure (children) | Fever, age <5 y, brief generalized tonic‑clonic activity | Fever present; resolves quickly; no prior epilepsy |
The occurrence of a single seizure or of febrile seizures does not necessarily imply the diagnosis of epilepsy
● Febrile seizures occur in 2% to 4% of the pediatric population.

qs.q: What is the defining age range for diagnosing febrile seizures in children?
o: Ages 12 to 72 months
Ages 6 to 60 months
Ages 3 to 36 months
Ages birth to 18 months
qs.e: Febrile seizures typically occur between the ages of 6 and 60 months, with a peak incidence around 12 to 18 months. An age range of 3 to 36 months would miss older toddlers who still fit the classic epidemiological criteria.

qs.q: How is a simple febrile seizure clinically distinguished from a complex febrile seizure?
o: They are always associated with central nervous system infections.
They are focal and last longer than 30 minutes.
They are primary generalized, last up to 15 minutes, and do not recur within 24 hours.
They recur multiple times within 24 hours regardless of duration.
qs.e: A simple febrile seizure is defined as a primary generalized attack lasting a maximum of 15 minutes and not recurring within 24 hours. A seizure that is focal, prolonged (>15 min), or recurrent within 24 hours is classified as complex.

qs.q: What term describes a febrile seizure that continues for a duration greater than 30 minutes?
o: Febrile status epilepticus
Complex febrile recurrence
Dravet syndrome
Refractory epilepsy
qs.e: Febrile status epilepticus is specifically defined as a febrile seizure lasting longer than 30 minutes. Refractory epilepsy refers to difficult-to-treat seizures seen in conditions like FIRES rather than the duration of a single acute event.

qs.q: A concerned parent asks about the long-term cognitive prognosis after their toddler experiences a simple febrile seizure. What is the expected neurocognitive outcome for this child?
o: A progressive decline in overall IQ scores
Marked impairment in verbal memory tasks
Persistent behavioral and attention deficits
Normal cognitive and scholastic development
qs.e: Children with simple febrile seizures show no increase in abnormalities of behavior, neurocognitive function, or scholastic performance compared to controls. Cognitive deficits are generally only seen in children who develop subsequent unprovoked epilepsy.

qs.q: Genetic testing is performed on an infant presenting with prolonged febrile seizures and developmental stagnation following routine childhood immunizations. What is the significance of identifying a pathogenic SCN1A mutation in this clinical context?
o: It proves that the immunization triggered a permanent metabolic encephalopathy
It indicates the condition is a genetic channelopathy rather than vaccine-induced
It demonstrates that prophylactic antibiotic therapy was omitted prematurely
It confirms the presence of an acute post-infectious autoimmune encephalitis
qs.e: Patients presumed to have suffered from vaccine encephalopathy often turn out to have Dravet syndrome mutations, indicating their condition is genetic rather than caused by the vaccine. This finding has raised doubts about the existence of true vaccine encephalopathy.

qs.q: What is the recommended approach regarding electroencephalogram (EEG) evaluation for a child presenting with a first simple febrile seizure who is otherwise neurologically healthy?
o: An EEG need not be performed as part of the evaluation.
An EEG is mandatory if the child is under 12 months of age.
An EEG should be performed within 24 hours to predict recurrence.
An EEG must be performed immediately for at least 60 minutes.
qs.e: If the child is presenting with the first simple febrile seizure and is otherwise neurologically healthy, an EEG need not be performed as part of the evaluation because it does not predict future epilepsy or recurrence.

qs.q: Why are EEGs performed within two weeks of a febrile seizure often delayed or interpreted with caution?
o: They require general anesthesia which is contraindicated shortly after.
They can trigger immediate status epilepticus if performed too early.
They invariably show absolute suppression of background electrical activity.
They frequently display nonspecific slowing, usually posteriorly, leading to misinterpretation.
qs.e: EEGs performed within two weeks of a febrile seizure often reveal nonspecific slowing, usually in the posterior regions, meaning they are frequently delayed or repeated after two weeks have passed to avoid erroneous conclusions.

qs.q: Which viral infections are frequently noted in the context of febrile seizures and account for approximately 30% of cases presenting as febrile status epilepticus?
o: Varicella-zoster and Cytomegalovirus
Rotavirus and Adenovirus infections
Human herpesvirus 6B (HHV-6B) and HHV-7
Influenza A and Respiratory Syncytial Virus
qs.e: Febrile seizures frequently occur in the context of HHV-6 infections, and in patients presenting specifically with febrile status epilepticus, HHV-6B and HHV-7 account for 30% of the cases. Other common triggers include otitis media and enteroviruses.

es.q: Define simple and complex febrile seizures and state the age range for their occurrence.
es.m:
**Definition of Simple Febrile Seizure:**
- Primary generalized, usually tonic-clonic attack.
- Lasts for a maximum of 15 minutes.
- Does not recur within a 24-hour period.
- Occurs with a temperature of 38°C or higher.
- No history of prior afebrile seizures.

**Definition of Complex Febrile Seizure:**
- Prolonged duration (>15 minutes).
- Focal in nature.
- Recurs within a 24-hour period.

**Age Range:**
- Occurs between 6 and 60 months of age.
- Peak incidence is between 12 and 18 months.

es.q: List the genetic factors and cytokine dysregulations associated with febrile seizures.
es.m:
**Genetic Factors:**
- Positive family history is common; can be autosomal dominant or polygenic.
- Associated genes include SCN1A, SCN1B, SCN9A, and CPA6.
- GEFS+ is an autosomal dominant syndrome with variable phenotype.
- Dravet syndrome is often caused by de novo SCN1A mutations (loss of function).

**Cytokine Dysregulation:**
- Dysregulation between proinflammatory (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8) and anti-inflammatory (ILR-1A) cytokines.
- Decreased ILR-1A/IL-8 ratio suggests a proinflammatory state.
- This ratio may predict hippocampal abnormalities on MRI after febrile status epilepticus.

es.q: Outline the indications for performing a lumbar puncture in a child presenting with a febrile seizure.
es.m:
**Mandatory Indications:**
- All infants younger than 6 months of age.
- Child appears ill.
- Clinical signs or symptoms of concern at any age.

**Optional Indications:**
- Children aged 6-12 months with unknown or deficient immunization status for H. influenzae type b and S. pneumoniae.
- Children who have been pretreated with antibiotics.

**Findings:**
- Nontraumatic LP in febrile status epilepticus rarely shows pleocytosis (<3 nucleated cells).
- Pleocytosis suggests bacterial or viral infection.

es.q: Describe the role of Electroencephalogram (EEG) in the evaluation of febrile seizures.
es.m:
**General Role:**
- Not required for the first simple febrile seizure in a neurologically healthy child.
- Does not predict future recurrence of febrile seizures or epilepsy.
- Should be restricted to cases where epilepsy is highly suspected to delineate type.

**Timing and Interpretation:**
- EEGs within 2 weeks often show nonspecific posterior slowing.
- If indicated, delay or repeat EEG after 2 weeks have passed.
- Spikes during drowsiness (especially >4 years) do not predict later epilepsy.
- Must be performed for at least 20 minutes in wakefulness and sleep to avoid misinterpretation.

ai.title: Febrile Seizures
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A brief generalized tonic‑clonic event in a child 6 months‑5 years with fever and an obvious source, resolving quickly and not indicating epilepsy.

sections.p: A febrile seizure is a brief generalized tonic‑clonic event in a child 6 months‑5 years with fever, no prior epilepsy, and an identifiable source of infection.
All febrile seizures are considered simple unless they are prolonged, focal, or recur within 24 h. No formal staging beyond these criteria.
In low‑resource settings the leading infections are respiratory tract infections, malaria, and diarrhoeal disease. Other contributors include HIV, TB, and sickle cell crises.
The child has a sudden loss of consciousness, stiffening of limbs, and possible frothing at the mouth. The event lasts less than 15 min and the child recovers fully.
Investigations are guided by clinical suspicion of a serious underlying infection or metabolic disturbance.
Seizure lasting >15 min, focal features, or recurrence within 24 h warrants urgent evaluation for meningitis, encephalitis, or metabolic crisis.
Treat the underlying infection, provide supportive care, and monitor for recurrence. Antipyretics are used to reduce fever but are not seizure prophylaxis.
b: Give paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever
Start antibiotics if bacterial infection suspected

sections.p: Educate caregivers about fever management, vaccination, and when to seek care. No routine prophylaxis is recommended for simple febrile seizures.
Seizures due to meningitis, encephalitis, hypoglycaemia, or epilepsy may mimic febrile seizures but differ in duration, focality, and recurrence.
A normal CSF in early bacterial meningitis can occur; repeat lumbar puncture may be needed. Malaria parasitemia can be low in early infection.
b: False‑negative malaria rapid test in low parasitaemia

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of meningitis (neck stiffness, bulging fontanelle)

faq.q: Do febrile seizures increase the risk of epilepsy?
faq.a: A single simple febrile seizure does not increase epilepsy risk; recurrence raises the risk modestly.
No; antipyretics reduce fever but do not prevent seizures.

faq.q: What is the best first‑line antipyretic in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Paracetamol is preferred due to safety and availability.

exam: A 3‑year‑old presents with a brief generalized seizure during a fever; what is the next best step? — Assess for meningitis: check neck stiffness, perform lumbar puncture if indicated.

How would you differentiate a simple febrile seizure from a focal seizure? — Simple seizures are brief (<15 min), generalized, and non‑recurrent; focal seizures have focal onset, may last longer, and can recur.
Why is a rapid malaria test important in this setting? — Malaria can precipitate seizures; a positive test directs antimalarial therapy.
What is the management of a seizure lasting 20 min in a febrile child? — Treat as status epilepticus: give benzodiazepine, then antiepileptic if needed, and investigate for underlying cause.
When is an EEG indicated after a febrile seizure? — If the child has recurrent seizures or atypical features, to rule out epilepsy.
Why should you avoid giving phenobarbital as prophylaxis for simple febrile seizures? — It has no proven benefit and carries risk of sedation and hepatotoxicity.
